issues.title: Set up repository tooling, the compose stack and CI
issues.body:
## User story

As a contributor, I want every toolchain in a container behind `make` and one test gate that CI runs too, so that Rotor works the way Exciter, Armature and Stator do from the first commit.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `make help` lists the targets; `make up` starts Postgres, Valkey, Keycloak with the realm `dynamo` and OpenBao in dev mode configured by an init script; the api joins in #3 and the web app in #5; Go 1.26, Python 3.13 and Node run in containers only
- [ ] `./run-tests.sh` runs the layers shell, check-format, check-go, check-python, check-web, test-integration and test-e2e (a layer without a make target yet is skipped); `--list` names them; the quick gate leaves the stack layers to CI and `ROTOR_GATE=full` runs them
- [ ] `.github/workflows` runs every layer on each pull request and blocks the merge when one fails
- [ ] CONTRIBUTING.md, CLAUDE.md, SECURITY.md, NOTICE, CHANGELOG.md and VERSION exist, adapted from Exciter (branches `<type>/<issue>-<slug>` via `gh issue develop`, Conventional Commits, `--no-ff` merges)
- [ ] `.claude/skills/gh/SKILL.md` and `.claude/hooks/branch-guard.sh` are adapted from Exciter
- [ ] `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/feature.yml`, `bug.yml` (with optional Run ID and sandbox backend fields and a note to strip tokens from logs) and `config.yml` (blank issues off, vulnerability link to security advisories)
- [ ] `tests/test-stack.sh` checks that the issuer, client and secret in compose match the realm

## Tests

Shell: `run-tests.sh --list` and each layer on an empty project. Stack: `make up` comes up healthy and `tests/test-stack.sh` passes.

## Implementation

- Port `Makefile`, `mk/`, `run-tests.sh`, `deploy/docker-compose.yml`, `.github/workflows/ci.yml` and the `.claude/` hooks (Exciter has no `.githooks/`) from `Cloudster1/Exciter`, trimmed to Rotor's services.
- OpenBao dev container plus `deploy/openbao/init.sh` enabling KV v2, transit and JWT auth.

## Depends on

- nothing

issues.title: Record the architecture decisions: Go control plane, Python runner, OpenBao, delegation and sandboxes
issues.body:
## User story

As maintainers, we want the key decisions written down before code depends on them, so that every later issue follows one design and reviewers can point at the reason.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `docs/decisions.md` records the split: a Go control plane (api, worker, web) and a Python runner that executes LangGraph inside the sandbox
- [ ] It records delegation: Rotor is an OAuth 2.1 client of each tool; refresh tokens live only in OpenBao and never enter a sandbox; each run gets its own short-lived access tokens limited to the workflow's scopes intersected with the person's consent
- [ ] It records who a run acts as: a manual run acts as the person who starts it; a scheduled or event run acts as the trigger's owner and stops when that person's consent or account ends
- [ ] It records OpenBao auth: JWT/OIDC with a Keycloak service account for the control plane, Kubernetes auth for sandboxes
- [ ] It records sandboxes: one per run, kept while the run is active or waiting until an idle TTL, then destroyed and respawned from a checkpoint; gVisor RuntimeClass in production, a Docker backend for development only
- [ ] It records the runner channel (the runner dials out to the control plane over gRPC, so a sandbox takes no ingress), checkpoints owned by the control plane (the sandbox never reaches Postgres), the declarative spec with Python code nodes, and run events to the browser over SSE
- [ ] It lists alternatives and why they lost: an MCP gateway in the control plane instead of tokens in the sandbox, LangGraph's PostgresSaver, HashiCorp Vault, Kata Containers and Firecracker
- [ ] `docs/architecture.md` has a component and trust-boundary diagram

## Tests

Documentation only; reviewed in the pull request.

## Implementation

- Follow the format of `docs/decisions.md` in Exciter and Armature.

## Depends on

- nothing

issues.title: Sign in through the shared Keycloak realm dynamo
issues.body:
## User story

As someone using the suite, I want to sign in to Rotor with the same account I use for Exciter, Armature and Stator, so that there is one identity behind every workflow.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] OIDC authorization code flow with PKCE against the realm `dynamo`, client `rotor`, configured from `ROTOR_OIDC_*` environment variables (no local passwords); sessions are held in Postgres (`user_session`, SHA-256 of an opaque token, HttpOnly cookie `rotor_session`, SameSite Lax)
- [ ] Groups are synced at each sign-in; `rotor-administrators` maps to the administrator role
- [ ] OIDC Back-Channel Logout at `POST /api/v1/auth/oidc/backchannel-logout` ends the matching sessions; switching somebody off sets `is_active=false` and deletes their sessions (ending their triggers and tool connections follows in M1 and later)
- [ ] `deploy/keycloak/realm.json` adds the `rotor` client; `make realm-check` compares it with Dynamo's canonical copy and passes with a message while Dynamo holds none

## Tests

Integration: sign-in against Keycloak in compose, group mapping, back-channel logout. Playwright: sign in and out with axe.

## Implementation

- Adapt `backend/internal/oidc/` and `grouproles.go` from Exciter.

issues.title: Add test doubles for the tools and a suite profile with the real ones
issues.body:
## User story

As a tester, I want an OAuth and MCP stub kept honest by contract tests, plus the real Exciter pinned, so that integration tests mock nothing below the layer under test.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A `tool-stub` service serves any number of tools side by side under `/t/{tenant}`, each with RFC 8414 and RFC 9728 metadata, dynamic client registration, authorize (state, PKCE S256, `resource`, answering `iss`), a consent page, token and revoke with rotating refresh tokens and reuse detection, `POST /api/v1/mcp` and `GET /api/v1/meta`; a tenant without OAuth answers only the last two
- [ ] Tenants are created, inspected and disturbed through a control API reachable only inside the stack's network, never through the published port
- [ ] Contract tests check the stub against the siblings' vendored `api/openapi.json` files and a snapshot of Exciter's MCP `tools/list`
- [ ] A suite profile (`make suite-up`) runs the real Exciter, built from a pinned commit, beside Rotor's stack and its `dynamo` realm; Armature and Stator join once they are authorization servers (Cloudster1/Armature#280, praetorianer777/Stator#449)
- [ ] Tests against the real Exciter run in a CI job of their own, nightly and on pull requests labelled `suite`, outside the required checks

## Tests

Contract tests in the go layer; the stack layer checks the stub's service definition; the suite job checks Exciter's health and `mcp@1`.

## Implementation

- Stub written in Go as `backend/cmd/tool-stub` and `backend/internal/toolstub`, in the backend module so it shares its toolchain and image.
- `make tool-contracts` vendors the siblings' documents at pinned commits; `make tool-snapshots` records Exciter's `tools/list` from the suite.
- `mk/suite.mk` clones Exciter at the commit in `deploy/suite/EXCITER_REF` and runs its compose with an overlay that uses Rotor's Keycloak.

- #1
- #7

issues.title: Keep connection secrets in OpenBao
issues.body:
## User story

As an operator, I want every long-lived secret in OpenBao and nowhere else, so that a database dump or a compromised sandbox reveals no refresh token.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A Go client authenticates to OpenBao with JWT auth using a Keycloak client-credentials token of `rotor-control-plane` and renews its own token, logging in again when renewal ends
- [ ] KV v2 at `rotor/connections/{userID}/{toolID}` and `rotor/tools/{toolID}/client`; the mount requires check-and-set, and the client's API is typed so nothing outside it builds a path
- [ ] Policies live as code in `deploy/openbao/policies/*.hcl` and are applied by the compose init script and later the chart; the control plane may touch `connections` and `tools` and nothing else
- [ ] `/readyz` fails while OpenBao is sealed, uninitialized or unreachable
- [ ] Dev OpenBao keeps its data across restarts: a server with file storage, initialized and unsealed by its entrypoint
- [ ] Integration tests run against a real OpenBao; a test proves the `rotor_app` database holds no secret material (with #11, once a secret exists)

## Tests

Integration against OpenBao in compose: login and renew, CAS conflict, policy denial outside `connections` and `tools` (other KV paths, transit, `sys`), sealed readiness against a second, never-unsealed OpenBao (`openbao-sealed`) and an unreachable one. Stack layer: a secret survives a restart of OpenBao.

## Implementation

- New package `backend/internal/vault` using `github.com/openbao/openbao/api/v2`.
- Layout and policy as in `docs/api-contract-m1.md`.

## Depends on

- #3
- #7

Related: praetorianer777/Dynamo#6

issues.title: Mint a short-lived access token for a person and a tool
issues.body:
## User story

As the control plane, I need a narrow, short-lived access token per run, so that a sandbox never holds more than the run needs, for longer than it needs it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `Mint(user, tool, scopes)` refuses when the scopes are not within the person's consent, naming what is missing
- [ ] Only one refresh runs at a time per connection (advisory lock or Valkey lock); the rotated refresh token is written to OpenBao with check-and-set before the access token is used; a test runs 20 parallel mints without ending the grant
- [ ] Each run gets its own access token, never shared, so revoking it affects one run only
- [ ] When a tool cannot narrow a token without narrowing the whole grant (Exciter today), Rotor mints the consented scope, the runner enforces the narrower scope, and the run records "not narrowed at the tool"; narrowing at the tool follows the Exciter token-exchange issue
- [ ] The audit log records `token.minted` with tool, scopes, run and expiry, never the token

## Tests

Integration against `tool-stub` with reuse detection on: parallel mints, scope refusal, CAS conflict recovery. Against real Exciter: minted token works at `/mcp`.

## Implementation

- `backend/internal/connections/mint.go`; lock key per connection.

## Depends on

- #8
- #10
- #11

Related: Cloudster1/Exciter#235

issues.title: Compile a workflow into a LangGraph graph in the runner
issues.body:
## User story

As the runner, I turn a spec into a StateGraph, so that workflows are data and not code, and LangGraph handles orchestration, retries and interrupts.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `agent` becomes a LangChain tool-calling agent built with `init_chat_model`; `tool` becomes one MCP call with templated arguments; `router` becomes conditional edges; `approval` becomes `interrupt()`; `code` is handled by the code-node issue
- [ ] MCP over streamable HTTP via langchain-mcp-adapters with a bearer token per tool; the tool list is filtered to `allowTools`, and read-only bindings to tools with `readOnlyHint`
- [ ] `limits` map to the recursion limit and timeouts; a violation ends the run with a reason
- [ ] pytest runs workflows with a fake chat model against `tool-stub`

## Tests

pytest: one test per node type, tool filtering, limit violations.

## Implementation

- `runner/rotor_runner/compile.py`.

issues.title: Run Python code nodes
issues.body:
## User story

As an author, I want a small Python step when the declarative nodes are not enough, so that I don't need a new node type for each transformation.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `def run(state, ctx) -> dict` runs in a subprocess inside the sandbox without the tool tokens in its environment
- [ ] `ctx.call_tool` goes through the runner, which enforces `allowTools`
- [ ] Only preinstalled libraries are available (no installs at run time); per-node timeouts and memory limits apply
- [ ] Output must be JSON and is checked against the declared output schema; stdout and stderr become size-capped log events

## Tests

pytest: token absence in the subprocess environment, timeout, memory limit, schema refusal, disallowed tool refused.

## Implementation

issues.title: Build the runner protocol between control plane and sandbox
issues.body:
## User story

As the control plane, I need one well-defined channel to a sandbox, so that runs can be started, fed tokens, resumed, cancelled and watched.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The runner dials `RunnerControl` over TLS with a one-time bootstrap credential that is single-use and expires within minutes
- [ ] One bidirectional stream: control plane to runner `StartRun`, `Resume`, `Cancel`, `TokenGrant`; runner to control plane `Hello`, `Event`, `RequestToken`, `Heartbeat`, `Done`
- [ ] Sequence numbers and acknowledgements so a reconnect loses no event; missed heartbeats mark the sandbox lost
- [ ] Conformance tests run the Go server against the Python client

## Tests

Conformance suite; bootstrap reuse refused; reconnect replay.

## Implementation

- `backend/internal/runnerctl`; `runner/rotor_runner/control.py`.

- #4
- #13

issues.title: Start a workflow by hand and carry the run to its end
issues.body:
## User story

issues.body:
## What happens

1. The control plane reads a workflow's YAML with goccy/go-yaml, which reads a plain scalar with a colon inside a flow sequence nested in a flow mapping as a mapping: `{tool: exciter, scopes: [mcp:read]}` gives `scopes: [{mcp: read}]`. YAML 1.2, and the runner's ruamel.yaml, read the string `mcp:read`. So the control plane refuses, or misreads, a workflow the runner reads fine, and the golden fixtures do not catch it.
2. M1's not-found errors for a tool and a connection answer a bare noun (`ErrNotFound("tool")`) where every other refusal is a sentence that says what to do.

## Expected

- Go and Python read every YAML 1.2 document alike; a golden fixture holds them to the flow-style case.
- The not-found refusals are sentences.

issues.title: Find out whether OpenShell can isolate a run, on the kind cluster
issues.body:
## User story

As an operator of Rotor, I want to know whether NVIDIA OpenShell can isolate a run better than Rotor's own gVisor pods, before Rotor builds a backend for it.

OpenShell moves three things outside the sandbox that Rotor today does inside it, or does more coarsely:
- **Each binding's `allowTools`.** OpenShell can allow MCP `tools/call` by tool name, outside the sandbox. Today the runner, inside the untrusted boundary, filters the tools it offers.
- **Egress.** OpenShell filters per request, at L7 with TLS termination, instead of by Cilium hostname rules and NetworkPolicy.
- **Credentials.** The agent sees only placeholders. Today the model key and run tokens reach the runner's memory through OpenBao wrapping tokens.

What we know so far, from the OpenShell docs for v0.1.5 (Apache 2.0):
- **Parts:** a gateway, a supervisor per sandbox outside the agent's boundary, and the sandbox. The agent runs non-root, without capabilities, under Landlock and seccomp. If the supervisor is lost, the agent is frozen.
- **On Kubernetes:** a Helm chart, which needs the Agent Sandbox controller and a CNI that enforces NetworkPolicy. Each sandbox is a workload pod plus a supervisor pod.
- **Kernel needs:** Landlock ABI 3 (Linux 6.2+), seccomp user notification with ADDFD, and `process_vm_readv`.
- **Runtime class:** Kata is documented through `runtime_class_name`; gVisor is not mentioned.

This spike answers what the docs leave open, so that #119 to #122 can be corrected or closed.

## Acceptance criteria

- On this checkout's kind cluster (Cilium), these run beside Rotor's chart, each pinned to a release at least two weeks old:
  - the Agent Sandbox controller and its CRDs;
  - the OpenShell chart (`oci://ghcr.io/nvidia/openshell/helm-chart`).
- A throwaway Go program on the pinned SDK (`github.com/NVIDIA/OpenShell/sdk/go/openshell/v1`) starts the runner image in an OpenShell sandbox, and one run reaches its end.
- A new section of `docs/decisions.md` answers each question, with what was measured:
  1. **Isolation.** Does the supervisor admit a workload under gVisor (Landlock, seccomp user notification)? If not, does it under Kata, and what would Rotor lose without gVisor?
  2. **The runner protocol.** Does gRPC with mTLS to the api's runner port pass as a `tcp` endpoint with `tls: skip`?
  3. **Code nodes.** Do they still start under Landlock? They run under the same Python interpreter as the runner, so per-binary rules cannot tell them apart; what does that mean for #120?
  4. **Credentials.** Can a provider update reach a long-running runner? The docs say a process keeps the credential revision it started with, but Rotor mints tokens while a run goes on.
  5. **Cost.** How long to the first event, against a gVisor pod? How many pods and resources does a run cost?
  6. **Secrets at rest.** Can short-lived values be kept off the gateway's database, using the credential driver for Kubernetes Secrets? Rotor's rule is that secrets never land in a database.
- The outcome is go or no-go. With go, the bodies of #119 to #122 are corrected from the findings; with no-go, they are closed with the reason.

## Tests

None in the gate: the spike leaves a decision, not code. The commands that set the cluster up go into the decision, so they can be run again.

## Implementation

- Use `make kind-up` and the chart install test's setup in `scripts/kind/` as the starting point.
- Add `M11 OpenShell sandboxes` to the milestone list in `.claude/skills/gh/SKILL.md` on this issue's branch.
- Docs consulted:
  - [architecture](https://docs.nvidia.com/openshell/latest/about/architecture)
  - [Kubernetes setup](https://docs.nvidia.com/openshell/latest/kubernetes/setup)
  - [runtimes](https://docs.nvidia.com/openshell/latest/how-it-works/sandboxes/runtimes)
  - [network rules](https://docs.nvidia.com/openshell/latest/how-it-works/policies/network-rules)
  - [providers](https://docs.nvidia.com/openshell/latest/how-it-works/providers/overview)
  - [Go SDK](https://docs.nvidia.com/openshell/latest/sdk/go)
  - [support matrix](https://docs.nvidia.com/openshell/latest/about/support-matrix)

## User story

As an operator, I want Rotor to start each run in an NVIDIA OpenShell sandbox when I choose to. Then I get OpenShell's supervisor and policy enforcement around every run, and today's gVisor pods stay the default for everyone else.

## Acceptance criteria

- `ROTOR_SANDBOX_BACKEND=openshell` makes the worker start, list, check and end sandboxes through an OpenShell gateway; `kube` and `docker` work as before.
- **Settings** (`backend/internal/config/sandbox.go`):
  - `ROTOR_OPENSHELL_ADDR`, `ROTOR_OPENSHELL_WORKSPACE` and `ROTOR_OPENSHELL_CA_FILE`;
  - OIDC client credentials of a realm client, which the gateway trusts.
- **Refusals:** outside development the api and the worker refuse to start without TLS to the gateway and a user credential. The error says what to set.
- **Each sandbox:**
  - carries the `rotor.dev/sandbox`, `rotor.dev/stack` and `rotor.dev/run` labels;
  - gets `Spec.Env` and `Spec.SecretEnv`, the bootstrap token kept as the gateway keeps secrets;
  - gets the limits, and the policy #120 renders.
- **Status** maps OpenShell's phases (Provisioning, Starting, Ready, Stopping, Stopped, Completed, Error, Deleting, Unknown) to Rotor's states (starting, running, exited, unknown).
- **The worker's passes** (reconcile, expire, teardown) work unchanged. OpenShell has no `activeDeadlineSeconds`, so the deadline stays with the worker.

## Tests

- **Unit:** the phase mapping and the label filter; `config_test` cases for the new settings and refusals.
- **Integration:** against an OpenShell gateway on its Docker driver in the compose stack, under a compose profile (`openshell`) so the default stack and gate are unchanged. A run reaches its end, and a sandbox no live run keeps is destroyed by the next pass.
- **Kubernetes:** a `make test-kube` variant on kind with the OpenShell chart, as set up in the spike.

## Implementation

- **The backend:** `backend/internal/sandbox/openshell`, implementing `sandbox.Backend` (`backend/internal/sandbox/sandbox.go`):
  - Spawn is `Sandboxes().Create` with `SandboxTemplate.Image`, `Environment`, labels and `Policy`, then `WaitReady`;
  - Status is `Get`, List is a paged list filtered by labels, and Destroy is `Delete`.
- **The SDK:** `github.com/NVIDIA/OpenShell/sdk/go`, pinned to a release at least two weeks old, the same release as the gateway. It goes in `NOTICE` if any code is adapted.
- **Wiring:** the backend is chosen in `cmd/worker` beside `docker` and `kube`. Constants go in `backend/internal/config`.
- **Docs:** [Go SDK](https://docs.nvidia.com/openshell/latest/sdk/go), [gateway authentication](https://docs.nvidia.com/openshell/latest/how-it-works/gateways/authentication), [runtimes](https://docs.nvidia.com/openshell/latest/how-it-works/sandboxes/runtimes).

issues.title: Hold each run's network access to what its workflow declares, outside the sandbox
issues.body:
## User story

As a person whose run reads content an attacker may have written, I want the sandbox's way out to allow only what the workflow declared, checked outside the sandbox. Then a run that has been talked into something cannot call a tool its binding does not allow, even with the runner subverted.

Today each binding's `allowTools` and read-only access are applied by the runner, inside the untrusted boundary, and egress is held by Cilium hostname rules and NetworkPolicy. OpenShell's supervisor can terminate TLS and check each MCP request by method and tool name before it leaves.

## Acceptance criteria

- On the `openshell` backend (#119), Spawn sends a policy rendered from the run's pinned workflow version. The policy allows nothing else:
  - **Each tool binding's MCP host and port:**
    - `protocol: mcp` and `enforcement: enforce`;
    - `initialize`, `notifications/initialized` and `tools/list` allowed;
    - `tools/call` allowed only for the tool names in `allowTools`;
    - for a read binding, only the tools that say they only read, as `internal/catalog` reads them today.
  - **The run's model provider:** its host, port and API path.
  - **Rotor's runner port**, as a `tcp` endpoint with `tls: skip`: the runner's mTLS stays end to end.
  - **OpenBao**, only while #121 has not replaced unwrapping.
- **Who may connect:** each rule names the runner's binaries, by real path. The spike's finding on code nodes decides whether code nodes get a rule of their own.
- **Denials:** a `policy_denied` answer reaches the run's timeline as an event, and the audit log as `sandbox.denied`, naming the host and tool, never a credential.
- **Docs:** `docs/threat-model.md` records which checks moved outside the sandbox.

## Tests

- **Unit:** the renderer, covering a read binding, a write binding behind an approval, two bindings on one host, and a workflow without tools.
- **Integration:**
  - a code node calls a tool outside its binding's `allowTools`, and the supervisor refuses the call, not the runner;
  - a request to a host no binding names is refused;
  - both refusals are on the timeline and in the audit log.

## Implementation

- **The renderer:** a package of its own beside the backend, such as `backend/internal/sandbox/openshell/policy`. It reads `internal/workflow` spec types and the tool records in `internal/tools`.
- **Denials** come from OpenShell's sandbox logs or its OCSF export, whichever the spike shows is reliable: [logging](https://docs.nvidia.com/openshell/latest/observability/logging), [OCSF JSON export](https://docs.nvidia.com/openshell/latest/observability/ocsf-json-export).
- **Docs:** [network rules](https://docs.nvidia.com/openshell/latest/how-it-works/policies/network-rules), [policy schema](https://docs.nvidia.com/openshell/latest/how-it-works/policies/schema). The policy prover ([prover](https://docs.nvidia.com/openshell/latest/how-it-works/policies/prover)) may check rendered policies in a test.
- **Related:** #32. A deny rule can hold a write back before it reaches the tool, which may serve that issue once Exciter#235 ships.

## Depends on

#119.

issues.title: Keep a run's tokens and the model key out of its OpenShell sandbox
issues.body:
## User story

As a person whose run acts in a tool as me, I want my access tokens and the installation's model key never to enter the sandbox. Then a run that has been talked into something has no credential to leak, and can use one only on the endpoint it belongs to.

Today the control plane mints each binding's token as the run asks for one, keeps it in OpenBao and sends a wrapping token that opens once. The runner unwraps it and holds the token in memory; the provider key travels the same way. OpenShell providers give the agent an opaque placeholder instead. The supervisor puts the real value in only on requests to endpoints the provider is bound to.

## Acceptance criteria

- **Per binding:** on the `openshell` backend (#119), when a run starts or its runner asks for a binding's token, the control plane:
  - mints the access token as today (`internal/connections`);
  - stores it as an OpenShell provider bound to that tool's MCP host, port and path;
  - attaches the provider to the run's sandbox.
  The runner receives a placeholder.
- **The model provider's key** is attached the same way:
  - for Anthropic and OpenAI, with OpenShell's built-in profiles;
  - for Azure OpenAI and OpenAI-compatible endpoints, with a profile Rotor imports for that host.
- **Rotation:** a token minted again during a run reaches the runner as the spike found it can. Either a provider update reaches the running process, or the runner starts each tool session in a new process. The decision is recorded.
- **When the run ends** (or its connection ends, or its person is switched off), the providers are detached and deleted, and the tokens are revoked at their tools, as today.
- **What stays the same:**
  - refresh tokens stay in OpenBao alone;
  - the gateway keeps only short-lived values, in the credential driver for Kubernetes Secrets where the spike found it works.
- **Docs:**
  - `docs/decisions.md` records where the gateway keeps them and why that meets the secrets rule;
  - `docs/threat-model.md` is updated;
  - `SECURITY.md`'s claims for tokens and the sandbox say what holds on this backend.

## Tests

- **Integration**, on the `openshell` backend:
  - a run's tool calls and model calls succeed;
  - the runner's environment and `/proc` hold no real token or key;
  - a request carrying the placeholder to a host no provider is bound to fails closed;
  - after the run, the gateway lists none of its providers, and the tool counts the revocations (tool-stub stats).
- **Unit:** the provider records Rotor builds for each kind of binding and model provider.

## Implementation

- Calls go through the pinned Go SDK's provider and attachment APIs, behind `internal/runnerctl`'s token path, so the `kube` backend keeps OpenBao wrapping.
- Docs: [providers](https://docs.nvidia.com/openshell/latest/how-it-works/providers/overview), [profiles](https://docs.nvidia.com/openshell/latest/how-it-works/providers/profiles), [inference](https://docs.nvidia.com/openshell/latest/how-it-works/inference), [Kubernetes credential storage](https://docs.nvidia.com/openshell/latest/kubernetes/setup).

## Depends on

#119, and the answer of #118 on rotation and secrets at rest.

issues.body:
## User story

As a person who sets up a trigger, I want it agreed before it is built how a trigger leaves events out, how it ignores what its own runs wrote, and how a few named writes may happen without an approval, so the M12 workflows rest on one agreement.

## Acceptance criteria

- **Contract:** `docs/api-contract-m12.md` agrees, as `docs/api-contract-m6.md` did:
  - the condition operators `notEquals`, `notIn` and `absent`;
  - the write ledger: what a run reports for each write, how long it is kept, and how a delivered event is matched against it;
  - the binding field `unattended: [call]` and the trigger body's `allowUnattended`, with the problems `unattended_not_allowed` and `unattended_widened`, and the administrator setting that forbids unattended writes.
- **Pending operations:** operations not built yet are in `api/openapi.json` with `pending: true` and answer 501.
- **Decision:** a section of `docs/decisions.md` says why named unattended writes are acceptable before #32:
  - the person's review in Exciter stays the gate;
  - a call that decides a review is still refused;
  - every such write is audited;
  - an administrator can forbid them.

issues.title: Give a step a workspace with the run's branch checked out
issues.body:
## User story

As a workflow author, I want an agent or code step to work in a checkout of the run's branch, reading and editing files and running commands, so a coder can write code and a reviewer can read it.

## Acceptance criteria

- **The block:** `workspace: {repository, branch, image, access}` on agent and code nodes, as #131 agreed. `image` must be one an administrator allows.
- **The sandbox** (`docs/decisions.md`, #132):
  - a run whose pinned version has workspace nodes gets, beside the runner, one toolchain container per image those nodes name; other runs get today's pod;
  - the toolchain container's entrypoint is Rotor's exec agent, which an init container copies in, so any allowed image works as it is;
  - the runner reaches the agent over the pod's loopback with a secret per sandbox, delivered like the bootstrap token, so code nodes cannot call it;
  - the toolchain container is hardened as the runner is: non-root, read-only root, no capabilities. Its caches (`HOME`, `TMPDIR`, `GOCACHE`, `GOMODCACHE` and the like) are an ephemeral volume of 4 GiB on disk, the work tree a memory volume of 1 GiB, and its memory 3 GiB unless an administrator sets more for the image.
- **Tools:**
  - an agent gets `list_files`, `read_file` and `search`;
  - with `access: write`, also `write_file` and `edit_file`;
  - every path stays inside the work tree and no tool follows a symbolic link, since the toolchain can plant one pointing at the runner's own files;
  - `run_command` runs an argv, without a shell, in the toolchain container through the agent: a timeout of 15 minutes unless the call says, at most the run's, kills the command's process group; the output keeps its first and last 32 KiB of 64 KiB.
- **The branch:**
  - at its start the runner fetches only the run's branch, at depth 1, with dulwich, into a git directory only the runner mounts, and checks it out into the work tree, which has no `.git`;
  - with `access: write` the runner commits what changed (a link as a link) and pushes at the end, with the run's Armature token, which never reaches the toolchain container;
  - a step that fails pushes nothing.
- **Nothing else is kept** between steps:
  - each step has its own directory in the work tree volume, removed at its end with the toolchain's caches;
  - the agent then ends every process of its container, those that left their process group included;
  - a waiting run holds no workspace.
- **Egress:** Armature's host, git included, the run's other tools, the model provider, and one package mirror host an administrator sets, passed to the toolchain as `GOPROXY`, `GOSUMDB` and `npm_config_registry`. The public Go proxy is not offered, since it needs every Cloud Storage bucket.
- **Fences:** text read from files is fenced as data, like any tool's answer.

## Tests

- **Unit:** the tools against a temporary checkout, a planted link refused among them; the agent's timeout, output cap and reset.
- **Integration:** in compose, against a test git server, with the toolchain container in the runner's network namespace, the agent as an image mount and a fixture repository without dependencies: a write step pushes, and a read step cannot.
- **Kube:** the same under gVisor on the kind cluster (`make test-kube`).

## Implementation

- The agent: a small Go command of its own, in an image of Rotor's; `scripts/kind/workspace-trial.sh` and `scripts/kind/workspace-trial/agent` in commit 3d350d8 are the trial's version.

## User story

As a product owner, I want a workflow that takes a feature specified in Exciter, writes its test specification and test cases, implements or updates the code and its tests, and repeats code, security, test and requirements reviews until every reviewer agrees. Then I get a pull request I can trust, and a trace from the requirements to passing tests.

- **The workflow:** `examples/implement-feature.yaml`, started by a person with:

  - `featureKey`, a section or a requirement;
  - the test section;

- **Test design loop**, at most 3 rounds, then a person decides:
  - a test designer writes or updates the test specification and its cases;
  - a test reviewer checks that every requirement is covered and every case can be verified.
- **Filing the tests:** the test cases go to Exciter as Test case requirements, linked to the requirements with `verifies`.
- **Implementation loop**, at most 5 rounds, then a person allows another round or stops:

  - a test step runs them;
  - four reviewers run in parallel, each with a read-only workspace: code review, security review, test run analysis, and conformance to the requirements;
  - a code node joins their verdicts, and any `changes` goes back to the coder with every finding.
- **Finish:**
  - a pull request through Armature, with the reviewers' summary;
  - the test results recorded in a test execution in Exciter;
  - a comment on the Armature issue.

issues.title: Let administrators cap the Stator pages a workflow may read
issues.body:
## User story

As an administrator, I want to set the highest Stator confidentiality level each workflow may read, and a default for every workflow, so that no workflow author can give their runs access to pages above it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The levels are Stator's: `public < internal < confidential < secret` (praetorianer777/Stator#595)
- [ ] An installation default, `internal` at first, that only administrators change
- [ ] A workflow's own cap, empty for the installation default, that only administrators change
- [ ] Only an administrator acting in person changes either: a member, the owner, and an assistant acting for an administrator are refused by the route (403) and again by the database for `rotor_app`
- [ ] `PUT /api/v1/workflows/{id}/confidentiality` (`admin: true`) takes a level or `null`; `PUT /api/v1/settings/confidentiality` sets the default
- [ ] The workflow summary returns `confidentiality` (`effective`, `source`: `workflow` or `default`) to everyone who may see the workflow
- [ ] Saving a new spec version leaves the cap untouched
- [ ] Audit actions `workflow.confidentiality_set` and `confidentiality.default_set`
- [ ] `api/openapi.json` and `web/src/api/schema.d.ts` regenerated; the agreement in `docs/api-contract-m14.md`
- [ ] `docs/decisions.md` records the choice: the first limit Rotor sets on top of a tool's own permissions, enforced by the tool through the run's token; `docs/architecture.md` (trust boundaries) and `docs/threat-model.md` follow
- [ ] `.claude/skills/gh/SKILL.md` lists `M14 Confidentiality levels`

## Tests

Unit: the route table and the admin flag in the OpenAPI document. Integration, as `TestAdministratorsForbidUnattendedWritesForEveryone` does: bob, owner and member, gets 403; alice, an administrator, gets 200 and the audit row is written; the same update straight through SQL as `rotor_app` is refused for the owner, for an assistant (`WithVia`) and for a member; a spec save keeps the cap.

## Implementation

- A migration after 01260: a singleton default table on the pattern of `01260_workspace_setting.sql`, and `workflow.stator_max_confidentiality`
- Row policies cannot guard one column, so a `BEFORE UPDATE` trigger refuses a change unless `current_actor_is_admin() AND current_actor_via() IS NULL`, as `workflow_owner_fixed` guards the owner
- Written through `db.WriteAdmin`, as `Archive` is in `workflows/save.go`

## Depends on

Nothing; the levels are agreed with praetorianer777/Stator#595.

issues.title: Hold each run's Stator reads to its workflow's cap
issues.body:
## User story

As an administrator, I want every run of a workflow to read Stator only up to the workflow's cap, enforced by Stator itself, so that a run, or anything that takes over its sandbox, cannot read a page above it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The cap is frozen on the run when it starts, so an administrator's later change does not alter a run that waits or runs
- [ ] Every Stator token minted for the run carries `stator_max_confidentiality`, the runner's and the trigger's `get_page` subject read alike
- [ ] A run with a Stator binding does not start when Stator does not advertise `confidentiality@1` or cannot exchange tokens; the refusal says what to update
- [ ] A triggered run whose subject page lies above the cap does not start; the trigger log says why, without the page's title
- [ ] The run page shows the cap the run read under; `token.minted` audits the cap carried

## Tests

Integration against the tool-stub: a run capped at `internal` reads an internal page and gets "not found" for a confidential page and for its child; a start without `confidentiality@1` is refused; a trigger skips a capped page; the frozen cap holds through an administrator's change. The suite repeats it against the real Stator.

## Implementation

- The Stator profile from #105 exchanges tokens (`SharedGrantToken`); `connections/exchange.go` takes the cap; `grant` in `runnerctl/startrun.go` and `hooks/triggers.go` pass it
- `runs.Service.Start` freezes the cap in a new `run` column and checks Stator's capability
- The tool-stub grows a Stator tenant with pages, parents and levels; its exchange accepts the cap and `get_page` and `search` honour it, held to the recorded `api/tools/stator/tools-list.json`

## Depends on

- #163
- #105
- praetorianer777/Stator#597

issues.title: feat: let a service account add tools and hook secrets
issues.body:
## User story

As the suite's operator, I want dynamo-connect to add Stator, Armature and Exciter to Rotor and hand it each tool's webhook secret, so that a fresh suite has Rotor wired to the tools without anyone clicking through Admin.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `GET /api/v1/tools`, `POST /api/v1/tools` and `GET`/`PUT /api/v1/tools/{toolID}/hook` accept `Authorization: Bearer` with an access token of the realm `dynamo` whose audience holds `rotor` and whose groups hold `rotor-administrators`
- [ ] Every other route still takes the session cookie only; a bearer token there is refused with a sentence that says which routes take one
- [ ] The origin check keeps applying to cookie writes and does not apply to bearer requests
- [ ] A token without the group, with the wrong audience or issuer, or expired is refused, and the refusal says what is missing
- [ ] Each change made with a bearer token is audited with the service account as the actor
- [ ] `GET /api/v1/tools` shows each tool's base URL and hook URL, so a caller finds a tool by its base URL and knows where to point the tool's webhook
- [ ] The development realm has a client `dynamo-connect`: a service account only, in `rotor-administrators`, with an audience mapper for `rotor`

## Tests

Integration: a client-credentials token of `dynamo-connect` adds a tool at the tool-stub and sets its hook secret; the same token is refused on `/api/v1/workflows`; tokens without the group or audience are refused. Unit tests for the token checks. The OpenAPI document names the bearer scheme on these operations.

## Implementation

- Today `backend/internal/httpapi/session.go` takes `rotor_session` only, and `assistant_auth.go` takes bearer tokens only at `/mcp`. Verify the token against the realm's JWKS as the assistant path does, and map the groups claim as `oidc/grouproles.go` does at sign-in.
- Dynamo's realm gets the same client, and its `dynamo-connect` uses it (praetorianer777/Dynamo#97).
- `docs/integration.md` names the routes and the token.

## Depends on

Nothing. A release after #167 carries it, since Dynamo pins only released images.

issues.title: feat: refuse to start a run when the installation runs no sandboxes
issues.body:
## User story

As a person using Rotor on an installation that runs no sandboxes, such as Dynamo's compose server, I want starting a run to be refused with a sentence that says why, so that I do not wait for a run that never starts.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] With `ROTOR_SANDBOX_BACKEND` empty, `POST` to start a run (and a trigger that would start one) answers with a refusal instead of 201 with a `queued` run; the sentence says this installation runs no workflows and that an administrator installs Rotor with sandboxes (the chart) to run them
- [ ] The web app shows that sentence where a run is started, and the workflow page says so before anyone presses Start
- [ ] A trigger that cannot start its run records why in the trigger log, once, without retrying forever
- [ ] `GET /api/v1/meta` or the settings an administrator sees say that runs are off, so dynamo-connect and Dynamo's server test can check it
- [ ] Nothing changes with a backend set; the worker's own message stays for the operator's log

## Tests

Integration: the api started without a backend refuses a run start and a trigger with the sentence; with the Docker backend the same start is accepted. Browser: the workflow page shows why Start is off.

## Implementation

Today `handleStartRun` needs only OpenBao, so the run is accepted and stays `queued`; the worker exits at `backend/cmd/worker/main.go:168` with "ROTOR_SANDBOX_BACKEND is not set, so the worker has nowhere to start sandboxes", which only the operator sees. The api reads the same setting (`backend/internal/config/sandbox.go`) and can refuse before the run row is written. The sentence lives in `web/src/strings.ts`.

Dynamo runs Rotor this way on a compose server (praetorianer777/Dynamo#96).

## Depends on

Nothing.

issues.title: feat: show hook urls at the address tools deliver to
issues.body:
## User story

As the suite's operator, I want the hook URL Rotor shows for a tool to be one that tool can reach, so that dynamo-connect can register each tool's webhook without rewriting addresses.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A setting `ROTOR_HOOKS_URL` (and the chart value beside it) names the base address tools deliver webhooks to, such as `http://rotor-api:8080` in a compose stack; without it, hook URLs keep using `ROTOR_APP_URL` as today
- [ ] `hookURL` in `GET /api/v1/tools` and the `url` of `GET /api/v1/tools/{toolID}/hook` use it, and so does the Admin page that shows the address to paste
- [ ] A value that is not an absolute http or https URL stops the start with a sentence that names the setting
- [ ] Rotor's own compose stack and the suite overlay set it to the api's address on the suite network, and a suite test delivers a real tool's event to it

## Tests

Unit tests for the setting; integration: with the setting, `hookURL` carries it and a ping to it is accepted; the suite test delivers an Armature or Exciter event to the address Rotor shows.

## Implementation

Today `hookURL` is built on `ROTOR_APP_URL` (#168), which in a compose stack is the browser's `http://localhost:<port>`; tools in other containers cannot reach that. `ROTOR_TOOLS_BACKCHANNEL` already maps the other direction, Rotor reaching tools. Dynamo's dynamo-connect registers the webhooks (praetorianer777/Dynamo#97) and runs Rotor's api as `rotor-api` (praetorianer777/Dynamo#95).

Nothing.
